title: Joining the Young Men's benevolent society
summary: Love explains how burial societies worked, why musicians joined them to get funeral jobs for the Excelsior Band, and how he quit after a fight over an election.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: I wanted you to tell us about that joining up with the young men, what that was like.

Well that was a society, you know. You pay so much, let me see, was it every week? Every quarter, they'd have a meeting just like the union. I don't know, I believe it was a dollar a quarter or something like that. I can't remember exactly, but anyhow, when you die they bury you, you see. They give you a funeral and your wife or who you may be made out to, your sister or something, she get so much money. But it wasn't very much a couple of hundred or something like that. But they bury you know. The time I got down there my wife had told the boys I was coming, you see. I had a job waiting for me in the Excelsior Band. And we was burying fellas every day, then two funerals a day. The fellas say, now why don't you get into the young men? That make the band more popular, you see. He said when you get in the band it'll always get your band to play for them, you know. And Peter was in one of them society too, Peter Burkhardt. I wanted to be right with the gang, you know, so I said I might as well get in one too. But sometime I'd get a funeral, you see. By being a member of that young man, you see. I'd get a funeral, give me the funeral, you know. So I'd ring up the boys, ring up the Excelsior Band. I said, I've got this one. Sometimes Willie Onfield would get a funeral uptown where he did that. See, he belonged to some of them societies too, you know. And his brothers too. All the musicians used to join for that purpose. Man, I joined that young man's society. I paid a dollar for that opportunity to join Gideon and that. So in the next quarter, they was voting, you know, for president one step or another. Them dudes right up there and start the fighting. I walked out. My wife said, what's the matter with them? I think a fellow named Willie Russell and the president, what they had at that time, they went together. Rear up to fight. One fellow had a pistol. I said, uh-uh. I said, I'll quit today. I just let them keep that dollar. I didn't want nothing to do with that society. I was there in it. I ain't never done nothing since but the union. We had a, what they call a union. We had a, not a union, they call it a pleasure club. We had a regular pleasure club. Didn't get nothing out of it. I stayed in there. I paid my dues and nothing until it was resolved. I drawed my money back. I got the money back off.
